citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (scan summary)
citations.excerpt: We scanned the HTTP headers of 217 million crawled web responses for text aimed at AI agents. Most point agents to llms.txt files and MCP servers, and 30 sites sent injection attempts.

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (prank share)
citations.excerpt: Prompt injection in HTTP headers is rare, and most of it is a joke. Of the 7,959 sites that sent a header aimed at AI, 30 tried to give an agent orders, and 22 of those were pranks.

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (agent test conditions)

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (test scope)

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (crawler identity limit)

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (AI client labelling)

citations.excerpt: When the same URL is requested by an AI agent (e.g., User-Agent = ChatGPT-User or PerplexityBot, or new AI browsers Atlas and Comet), the server delivers a fabricated negative profile .

citations.label: SPLX, AI-targeted cloaking against AI browsers (finding)

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (CCBot classified as AI bot)
citations.excerpt: 136 of the 139 detection sites in our scan sent a header saying they had classified the client, Common Crawl’s self-declared CCBot, as an AI bot. That only takes a user-agent match, and it is the first step cloaking needs.

citations.label: Signals Corps, prompt injection in HTTP headers (cloaking server test)
citations.excerpt: We built a small cloaking server to see what a manual check reveals. It sends ordinary headers to everyone and adds one more when the user agent contains a published AI fetcher name or the Accept header asks for Markdown first.
